enrichment.short_title: Confiscation certificate of inadequacy struck out as abuse
key_facts: The applicant was convicted of drug trafficking and a confiscation order of £750,000 was made based on assumed hidden assets abroad.
A court-appointed receiver recovered only £18,920.72.
The applicant applied under section 14 for a certificate of inadequacy of realisable property.
Deputy Judge Beatson QC struck out the application as an abuse of process because it sought to re-litigate the Crown Court's assessment of realisable assets.
The applicant did not attend the permission hearing in the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against an order striking out a section 14 certificate-of-inadequacy application; applicant absent at the oral hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; application dismissed as hopeless.
enrichment.ratio: An application for a certificate of inadequacy under section 14 of the Drug Trafficking Offences Act 1986 is an abuse of process where it seeks to go behind the Crown Court's finding on realisable assets, including assumed hidden assets, and the receiver's failure to recover assets does not constitute fresh evidence of inadequacy.
legal_issues: Whether a section 14 application can re-open the Crown Court's assessment of realisable assets
Distinction between Crown Court and High Court functions on confiscation under Re Norris
Application of Gokal v Serious Fraud Office to hidden assets
Whether issue estoppel or abuse of process applies despite no strict issue estoppel
linked_authorities: Government of the United States of America v Montgomery

confidence.notes: Outcome, statutory framework, abuse-of-process reasoning, and linked authorities are explicit in the judgment. The applicant's absence and permission refusal are clearly recorded.

enrichment.short_title: Claims Direct MLSS £395 fee held irrecoverable referral fee
key_facts: Second tranche of preliminary issues in detailed assessment test cases arising from the Claims Direct personal injury scheme.
Panel solicitors were required to pay £395 plus VAT to MLSS for every accepted case under the Operating Manual.
The court held MLSS, not Poole & Co, was the true introducer and the fixed fee was a referral fee.
Payment breached section 2(3) of the Solicitors Introduction and Referral Code 1990 and was irrecoverable from the paying party.
Several other tranche 2 issues were compromised, including counsel fee issues settled via the Bar and insurance premium transitional provisions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment test-case hearing on preliminary costs issues in Claims Direct litigation.
enrichment.outcome: MLSS £395 fee held to be an irrecoverable referral fee; breach of the Introduction and Referral Code; guidance given on counsel fees, counsel advice, insurance premiums, and Mobile Doctors Ltd administration charges.
enrichment.ratio: A compulsory fixed payment by a panel solicitor to obtain Claims Direct work through MLSS is a referral fee in breach of the Solicitors Introduction and Referral Code; such a fee is irrecoverable from the client and therefore from the paying party, although it does not necessarily taint the solicitor-client retainer itself.
legal_issues: Whether the £395 MLSS fee was a referral fee or payment for genuine support services
Consequences of breach of the Solicitors Introduction and Referral Code
Whether the solicitor-client retainer was rendered unenforceable
Treatment of MLSS fees as disbursements rather than profit costs
Recoverability of counsel and Mobile Doctors Ltd charges

confidence.notes: Core findings on the MLSS referral fee and code breach are explicit and heavily reasoned. Some compromised issues and guidance points are secondary to the live Issue 7 decision.

enrichment.short_title: Helicopter aerodrome disruption sentence reduced to two years
key_facts: The appellant, a helicopter pilot excluded from Coventry Airport after a dispute with the director, hovered at runway intersections and flew aggressively near the control tower on 12 October 2001.
Two departing jets and inbound aircraft were disrupted; staff evacuated the control tower fearing a deliberate attack shortly after 11 September 2001.
The appellant pleaded guilty to disrupting aerodrome services with intent and damaging property; he received three years' imprisonment.
He was a man of positive good character with low risk of reoffending, remorse, PTSD, and early guilty pleas.
The sentencing judge accepted custody was required but the Court of Appeal reduced the term to two years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Sentence appeal with leave of the single judge against a three-year custodial sentence in the Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; sentence reduced from three years to two years' imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Disrupting aerodrome services by deliberate and dangerous use of an aircraft warrants custody, but a sentence must still reflect strong mitigation including out-of-character conduct, remorse, good character, early plea, low reoffending risk, and the severe personal and professional consequences of imprisonment for the offender.
legal_issues: Whether a three-year sentence was manifestly excessive
Appropriate weight to be given to mitigation where custody remains necessary
Whether immediate release tailoring was appropriate

confidence.notes: Facts, offence, sentence, mitigation, and appellate reduction are all clearly stated. No complex statutory interpretation or external authority discussion.

enrichment.short_title: Enforcement of London arbitration award after long delay
key_facts: A London arbitration award of June 1983 for demurrage and detention remained unpaid despite part payments and long-running enforcement efforts in Romania.
Saville J granted an ex parte order under section 26 in January 1993, but the claimants did not serve it until August 2001 while Romanian proceedings continued.
The Romanian Supreme Court held enforcement in Romania failed on prescription and that the award was no longer executory in England after six years.
The court held there was no issue estoppel on English limitation because the Romanian decision on English law was not fundamental to that judgment.
Telex acknowledgments and part payments in 1986 and 1988 restarted the English limitation period, so enforcement was not time-barred in January 1993.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial court application to set aside an ex parte section 26 enforcement order, with a cross-application for permission to enforce a 1983 arbitration award as a judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants' application to set aside the Saville J order refused; claimants permitted to enforce the award, subject to further argument on interest.
enrichment.ratio: A foreign judgment on English limitation may found issue estoppel only if the determination was necessary and fundamental; where part payments and signed written acknowledgments restart limitation under sections 29 and 30 of the Limitation Act 1980, an ex parte section 26 application may remain enforceable despite long delay if service was withheld for legitimate reasons and the debtor was not prejudiced by abuse of process.
legal_issues: Issue estoppel arising from the Romanian Supreme Court's decision on English limitation
Whether the section 26 application was time-barred by January 1993
Effect of part payments and telex acknowledgments on limitation
Whether delayed reliance on an ex parte order was an abuse of process
Whether permission to enforce should be granted after more than six years
linked_authorities: Agromet Motoimport Ltd v Maulden Engineering Co (Beds) Ltd
Carl Zeiss Stiftung v Rayner & Keller Ltd (No. 2)

confidence.notes: Principal holdings on estoppel, limitation, abuse of process, and permission to enforce are clear. Final interest quantification was expressly left open.

enrichment.short_title: Co-op GlobalSTORE IT claim fails; ICL price adjustment succeeds
key_facts: Following the 2000 transfer of CRS engagements to CWS, CWS sued ICL over failed IT integration involving GlobalSTORE, ISS300/ISS400, SSM, and the Dividend loyalty scheme.
Negotiations for a GlobalSTORE contract never concluded, principally because the parties could not agree liquidated damages and other essential terms.
CWS claimed repudiatory breach and large damages for delays to the Harlech trial and Revised Dividend rollout; ICL counterclaimed under CRS Agreement price-adjustment provisions.
The court held no contract existed between CWS and ICL for the GlobalSTORE project and dismissed CWS's action.
ICL was entitled to £1,012,422 under the continuing CRS Agreement because the conditional price-adjustment provisions were triggered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of a major IT contract and damages claim with counterclaim after the CRS/CWS merger.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; ICL counterclaim succeeds for £1,012,422; numerous damages heads rejected on alternative findings.
enrichment.ratio: Where essential commercial terms such as liquidated damages, scope, and ICL standard conditions remain unresolved, negotiations for a major IT project do not give rise to a binding GlobalSTORE contract by conduct; without that contract CWS cannot recover project-abandonment losses, while ICL may still enforce separate existing contract price-adjustment rights under the earlier CRS Agreement.
legal_issues: Whether a binding GlobalSTORE contract was formed by conduct or variation of the CRS Agreement
Whether ICL repudiated any such contract
Recoverability of damages for delay in the Harlech trial and Revised Dividend rollout
Operation of CRS Agreement price-adjustment clauses
Misrepresentation and software-performance issues on alternative findings

confidence.notes: Primary dispositive findings on contract formation and the £1,012,422 counterclaim are explicit. The judgment is very long and the captured file appears truncated before later damages sections conclude.

enrichment.short_title: Personal tenant break clause lost after lease assignment
key_facts: Sketchley plc took a 25-year lease with a break option at year ten personal to Sketchley plc and not its successors or assigns.
The lease was assigned to Sketchley Retail Ltd in 1999 and later reassigned back to Sketchley Ltd, the renamed original tenant, in 2002.
Sketchley Ltd served a break notice for June 2003.
The landlord contended the personal break right was lost on the first assignment and could not revive on reassignment.
The court granted summary judgment for the landlord on a pure construction point.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Summary judgment application and counterclaim for declarations on the validity of a tenant break notice.
enrichment.outcome: Break notice held invalid; declarations made for the landlord.
enrichment.ratio: A break clause expressed to be personal to the original tenant and excluding successors in title and assigns does not revive when the lease is reassigned back to the renamed original tenant, because on reassignment it holds as assignee rather than in its original-tenant capacity.
legal_issues: Construction of a personal break clause excluding assigns and successors in title
Whether reassignment to the original tenant revives a lost break option
Commercial purpose of break rights tied to the original lessee only
index_terms: Olympia & York Canary Wharf Ltd v Oil Property Investments Ltd
Max Factor Ltd v Wesleyan Assurance Society
linked_authorities: Olympia & York Canary Wharf Ltd v Oil Property Investments Ltd
Max Factor Ltd v Wesleyan Assurance Society
St Martins Property Investments Ltd v CIB Properties Ltd
Brown & Root Ltd v Sun Alliance Ltd
Co-Operative Wholesale Society Ltd v National Westminster Bank plc

confidence.notes: Issue, clause wording, procedural context, and construction conclusion are all clearly stated and closely reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Permission to appeal on cargo bill of lading jurisdiction
key_facts: Welex arrested a vessel in Portugal to secure a cargo damage claim after shipment from Ukraine to Poland.
Rosa Maritime commenced London arbitration relying on a London arbitration clause said to be incorporated from a charterparty/fixture recap into the bill of lading.
Welex also pursued proceedings in Poland and David Steel J granted an anti-suit injunction.
The judge held fixture recap terms could be incorporated despite a blank charterparty date, differing from The Heidberg.
Permission to appeal was granted on incorporation, security availability in arbitration, and anti-suit discretion issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against two first-instance judgments on jurisdiction, bill-of-lading incorporation, and an anti-suit injunction.
enrichment.ratio: Important issues arise where a bill of lading may incorporate charterparty arbitration terms from an unsigned fixture recap despite a blank charterparty date, and where an anti-suit injunction is sought while foreign security and the existence of a London arbitration clause remain uncertain; such points can warrant permission to appeal even after substantial interlocutory costs.
legal_issues: Incorporation of charterparty arbitration terms into a bill of lading from a fixture recap
Whether The Heidberg prevents incorporation before a charterparty is reduced to writing
Availability of Portuguese arrest security in London arbitration
Discretion to grant or continue an anti-suit injunction where the arbitration clause was not initially known

confidence.notes: This is a permission decision rather than a full merits ruling, but the issues identified and the order granted are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: MIB not liable where passenger knew car uninsured
key_facts: Graham Akers, aged 16, was killed as a passenger in an uninsured car driven dangerously by Roy Thorne.
Relatives sued Thorne and the MIB under the 1988 MIB Agreement.
The driver and another passenger gave evidence that Thorne and Aaron Goldfinch said in the group that the car was not insured.
The trial judge was not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that Akers knew or ought to have known of the lack of insurance.
The Court of Appeal held the judge applied too stringent a standard and allowed the MIB appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: MIB appeal from a county court judgment holding it liable to satisfy the judgment against the uninsured driver.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declaration that the MIB is not obliged to satisfy the judgment or pay claimant costs of the hearing below.
enrichment.ratio: Under clause 6(1)(e) of the 1988 MIB Agreement, read consistently with White v White, the MIB exception applies where the injured passenger knew or, in the narrow sense of deliberately closing his mind after sufficient information, ought to have known the vehicle was uninsured; mere failure to inquire is insufficient.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'knew or ought to have known' in clause 6(1)(e) of the MIB Agreement
Application of White v White to uninsured passenger claims
Whether the trial judge's fact-finding on knowledge was open on the evidence

confidence.notes: Legal test, evidence review, and appellate reversal are clearly explained. Contributory negligence findings were not challenged on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: GMC data protection disclosure application refused
key_facts: Professor Aaalamani sought disclosure from the GMC of personal data under the Data Protection Act during related fitness-to-practise and judicial review proceedings.
The GMC had already disclosed extensive material and accepted further historic documents would be supplied.
The GMC relied on exemptions for legal professional privilege, third-party information, examination answers, and performance-test materials.
The court held the withheld categories were justified under the 1998 Act and consistent with the EU data protection directive framework.
Other pending Administrative Court proceedings were stayed pending the Privy Council appeal, with liberty to apply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under the Data Protection Act for disclosure of GMC-held personal data, with related case-management directions for other proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Data protection disclosure application dismissed; no order as to costs; other proceedings stayed pending Privy Council outcome.
enrichment.ratio: A data controller may withhold personal data where valid exemptions under the Data Protection Act 1998 apply, including legal professional privilege, third-party information under section 7(4), and examination materials under Schedule 7 paragraph 9; domestic exemptions implementing Article 13 of the data protection directive are to be applied rather than the directive alone.
legal_issues: Scope of the claimant's entitlement to personal data under section 7
Whether withheld GMC documents fell within Article 13 or domestic exemptions
Whether examination answers and performance-test materials were disclosable personal data
Case management of parallel GMC litigation pending Privy Council appeal

confidence.notes: The disclosure ruling and exemption analysis are clear. Underlying GMC merits and separate litigation disclosure issues were expressly reserved.

enrichment.short_title: Surveyor damages may use hindsight on stabilised property
key_facts: Mr and Mrs McKinnon bought a bungalow relying on a defective Homebuyer's survey that failed to identify significant structural movement defects.
They claimed damages equal to the difference between the purchase price and the value the property should have had if properly reported, about £93,000.
The defendant admitted negligence and that damages depended on the property's true value at the 1999 valuation date.
The preliminary issue assumed monitoring would show movement had ceased before purchase but that this could not have been established until after completion.
The court held hindsight evidence of stabilisation should be taken into account, reducing recoverable damages to about £37,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues in assessment of damages after admission of liability in a surveyor negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issues answered in the defendant's favour; damages to be assessed at April 1999 using hindsight evidence of the property's true condition.
enrichment.ratio: In surveyor negligence claims the prima facie measure of damages is the difference between the price paid and the property's value as it should have been described at the valuation date, but the overriding compensatory principle requires hindsight evidence to be admitted where later facts show the asset retained by the claimant was worth more than the defective-report valuation assumed.
legal_issues: Whether damages should ignore hindsight where stabilisation could not have been known at purchase
Interaction of the Phillips v Ward measure with the Livingstone compensatory principle
Application of the Bwllfa principle and avoided-loss reasoning in survey negligence cases
linked_authorities: Bwllfa and Merthyr Dare Steam Collieries Ltd v The Pontypridd Waterworks Co

confidence.notes: The preliminary issue, assumed facts, legal reasoning, and answers are all clearly set out on admitted liability.
